If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why their sleep clock shifts later in puberty, name what a short night costs (memory, mood, judgment, safety), and pick one lever they control, like morning light, a wake-up anchor, a caffeine cutoff, or the phone's bedtime. Nobody should leave feeling lectured about being lazy.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 5 minAnonymous tally, and the guess
  2. 6 minTired at 7 isn’t lazy: your clock moved
  3. 5 minWhat a short night costs, and you stop noticing
  4. 4 minThe weekend loop
  5. 5 minWhat keeps you up? Turn and talk, share out
  6. 5 minThe levers, and the caffeine guess
  7. 8 minThree tired students: Owen, Ava, Luis
  8. 4 minWork backward from your alarm
  9. 3 minEvery student, where else this shows up, close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

The tally, your clock moved, what it costs, the levers, one tired student, and work backward.

Before you teach
Never rank sleep.

Keep the hours tally anonymous. Don't praise the student who sleeps nine hours or joke about the one who sleeps four. Some students are proud of how little they sleep, and some are embarrassed. Both can stay private.

Many schedules aren't the student's to set.

Practice, a job, a long bus ride, siblings to watch, a shared room, a parent working nights. Present every tool as something to try within what they control. Blaming a student for a schedule the family needs will close the conversation fast.

Don't recommend melatonin or pills.

If students ask, the answer is: it's a timing signal, gummies vary a lot from the label, and a doctor or the school nurse should weigh in first. Don't suggest doses.

Rides are a safety topic for 9th graders.

Most 9th graders don't drive, but they ride with older teammates, siblings or parents who may be short on sleep. Make it clear that asking for a different ride is reasonable, and that calling a parent, caregiver or coach for one is a smart move.

Some sleep trouble is something more.

Weeks of not sleeping, exhaustion after a full night, loud snoring or gasping, or worry and sadness that keep a student up are worth a quiet word afterward and a walk to the nurse or a counselor. Don't ask about mood or safety in front of the class. If something comes up, pass it to a counselor that day.

If something at home is keeping a student awake.

Most of the time it's ordinary (a late dinner, a loud house). If a student hints that home isn't safe at night, thank them, don't press for details, and bring in a counselor that day.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Who keeps the house running at night.

Students live with one parent, two, a grandparent, foster or kinship caregivers, or move between homes. Some get younger siblings to bed while a parent or caregiver works. Say "the adults at home" and keep the "what does a school night look like at your place?" question private.

Work, money and space.

Some 9th graders babysit, help with a family business, or share a bedroom. Every lever in this lesson is free: morning light, a steady wake-up time, a caffeine cutoff, the phone across the room. A fan or earplugs help in a shared room. Don't suggest buying anything.

Family rhythms vary.

Dinner at 6 or at 9, tea or coffee at the table, a busy house late at night: norms differ from home to home. Treat every rhythm as normal and ask what students' own nights look like. Avoid "In X families" generalizations.

Faith can shape the clock.

Some students rise early or stay up for prayer, attend religious school after school, or fast during parts of the year. Treat those as part of the schedule they plan around. Prayer, meditation, or whatever grounds you can be a good wind-down.

Bodies and brains sleep differently.

Students with ADHD, autism, anxiety, a chronic illness, or medications may have a harder time with sleep. Some need a certain sound, darkness or routine. A student who dozes in class needs a check-in with the nurse or a counselor before any discipline.

Language and time zones.

Some students translate for family in the evening or call relatives in other countries late at night. That time matters. The take-home sheet is in plain language a student can share at home.

What the research says

In a 1998 study of 10th graders whose school started at 7:20, 12 of 25 fell straight into dream (REM) sleep on morning nap tests, a pattern usually seen in narcolepsy. During puberty, melatonin release starts later at night.

Carskadon et al., Sleep, 1998

Teens ages 13 to 18 need 8 to 10 hours of sleep. In 2023, about 77% of U.S. high school students got less than 8 hours on a typical school night.

American Academy of Sleep Medicine (Paruthi et al., 2016); CDC Youth Risk Behavior Survey, 2023

When Seattle moved high school start times from 7:50 to 8:45, students got about 34 more minutes of sleep a night and median grades rose 4.5%. One district, not a randomized trial.

Dunster et al., Science Advances, 2018

People kept awake all night were up to 40% worse at forming new memories the next day, with less hippocampus activity.

Yoo et al., Nature Neuroscience, 2007 (Harvard)

After a night without sleep, the amygdala reacted about 60% more strongly to upsetting images, and its connection to the prefrontal cortex weakened.

Yoo et al., Current Biology, 2007

Adults on 6 hours a night for two weeks kept getting worse on attention and memory tests, while their sense of sleepiness leveled off after a few days.

Van Dongen et al., Sleep, 2003

Caffeine taken 6 hours before bed still cost people about an hour of sleep, and they didn't notice.

Drake et al., Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine, 2013

Drivers who slept 4 to 5 hours had about 4 times the crash rate of those who slept 7 or more; under 4 hours, about 11 times. Melatonin gummies held 74% to 347% of the labeled dose.

Tefft, Sleep, 2018 (AAA Foundation); Cohen et al., JAMA, 2023
